readings.c1s1:
¶
'''web-press''' (web′pres), ''n.'' A printing-machine which is automatically supplied with its paper from a great web or roll: usually a rotary machine, but the name is given to newspaper printing-machines of different constructions, like those of Hoe, Marinoni, Walter, and others. See cut under ''printing-machine.''

'''web-saw''' (web′sâ), ''n.'' A frame-saw.
{{smaller block|The ''web-saw'', the glue-pot, the plane, and the hammer are the principal tools used. ''The Century'', XXXVII. 418.}}

'''webster†''' (web′stėr), ''n.'' [= Sc. ''wabster''; < ME. ''webstere'', ''webstar'', < AS. ''webbestre'', a female weaver, < ''webban'', weave: see ''web'' and ''-ster''. As with other ME. forms in ''-ster'' (strictly fem. in themselves), the word was also often regarded as masc. (cf. ''baxter'' and ''brewster''<sup>1</sup>, used as masc. in ME.). The name survives in the surname ''Webster''.] A weaver. ''Wyclif'', Job vii. 6.
{{smaller block|One witness says “a very good ''webster'' can scarcely earne fower pence a day w<sup>th</sup> weavinge.”
{{right|''Record Soc. Lancashire and Cheshire'', XI. 53.}}}}

'''websterite''' (web′stėr-īt), ''n.'' [So named in honor of Thomas ''Webster'' (1772–1844), a Scottish geologist.] Aluminite; hydrous tribasic sulphate of aluminium, found in Sussex, England, and at Halle in Prussia, in reniform masses and botryoidal concretions of a white or yellowish-white color.

'''Webster’s condenser.''' An apparatus consisting of two lenses, used in microscopy for intensifying the light thrown on the object.

'''web-toed''' (web′tōd), ''a.'' Web-footed.

{{smaller block|To ''wed'' her elm. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., v. 215.}}}}

{{smaller block|They . . . ''wedded'' his cause. {{right|''Clarendon.''}}}}
'''To wed with a rush ring.''' See ''rush''<sup>1</sup>.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To marry; contract marriage; become united as in matrimony.
{{smaller block|With Athulf child he ''wedde.''
{{right|''King Horn'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 9.}}
<poem>For to been a wyf he gaf me leve
Of indulgence, so it is no repreve
To ''wedde'' me if that my make dye.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 85.}}
<poem>Thought leapt out to ''wed'' with Thought
Ere Thought could wed itself with Speech.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, xxiii.}}}}

'''Wed.''' An abbreviation of ''Wednesday''.

'''wedbrek†''', ''n.'' [ME., < ''wed'' + ''break''.] An adulterer. ''Early English Psalter'', Ps. xlix. 18. (''Stratmann.'')

'''wedde†''', ''n.'' Same as ''wed''.

'''wedded''' (wed′ed), ''p. a.'' '''1.''' Married; united in marriage.
{{smaller block|Let wealth, let honour, wait the ''wedded'' dame.
{{right|''Pope'', Eloisa to Abelard, l. 77.}}}}
'''2.''' Of or pertaining to matrimony: as, ''wedded'' life; ''wedded'' bliss.—'''3.''' Intimately united or joined together; clasped together.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then fled she to her inmost bower, and there
Unclasp’d the ''wedded'' eagles of her belt.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Godiva.}}}}

'''wedde-fee''', ''n.'' See ''wed-fee''.

'''wedder<sup>1</sup>''' (wed′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''wed'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who weds.

'''wedder<sup>2</sup>''' (wed′ėr), ''n.'' A dialectal form of ''wether''.
readings.c3s1:
¶
'''wedding-bed''' (wed′ing-bed), ''n.'' The bed of a newly married pair.
{{smaller block|My grave is like to be my ''wedding bed.''
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., i. 5. 137.}}}}

'''wedding-cake''' (wed′ing-kāk′), ''n.'' A rich, decorated cake made to grace a wedding. {{smaller|It is cut and distributed to the guests, and portions of it are sent afterward to friends not present. Also ''bride-cake.''}}

'''wedding-cards''' (wed′ing-kärdz′), ''n. pl.'' In general, an invitation or notification sent out on the occasion of a marriage; specifically, two cards, one bearing the name of the bride and the other that of the groom.

'''wedding-chest''' (wed′ing-chest), ''n.'' A chest or coffer, usually of ornamental character, designed to contain the clothes and ornaments of a bride. Compare ''bridal chest'' (under ''chest''<sup>1</sup>), and ''cassone.''

'''wedding-clothes''' (wed′ing-klōᴛ̵ʜz′), ''n. pl.'' Garments made for the occasion of a wedding, especially those of the bride or the bridegroom, and either worn at the ceremony and festivities, or prepared as necessary for the changed conditions of life.

'''wedding-day''' (wed′ing-dā), ''n.'' The day of marriage.

'''wedding-dower''' (wed′ing-dou″ėr), ''n.'' A marriage-portion.
{{smaller block|Let her beauty be her ''wedding-dower.''
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iii. 1. 78.}}}}
readings.c3s2:
¶
'''wedding-dress''' (wed′ing-dres′), ''n.'' The dress worn by a bride at her wedding.

'''weddinger''' (wed′ing-ėr), ''n.'' [< ''wedding'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] A guest at a wedding; one of a wedding party. [Provincial.]

'''wedding-favor''' (wed′ing-fā″vo̤r), ''n.'' A bunch of white ribbons, or a rosette, etc., sometimes worn by men attending a wedding. ''Simmonds.''

'''wedding-feast''' (wed′ing-fēst), ''n.'' A feast or entertainment in honor of a wedding.

'''wedding-flower''' (wed′ing-flou″ėr), ''n.'' A plant, ''Moræa'' (''Iris'') ''Robinsoniana'' of Lord Howe’s Island, New South Wales, having white iris-like flowers sometimes 4 inches across.—{{smaller|'''Cape wedding-flower,''' ''Dombeya Natalensis,'' a South African shrub or small tree with showy flowers.}}

'''wedding-garment''' (wed′ing-gär′me̤nt), ''n.'' A garment such as is worn at a wedding ceremony or entertainment.
{{smaller block|And when the King came in to see the guests, he saw there a man which had not on a ''wedding garment.''
{{right|Mat. xxii. 11.}}
Is supper ready, the house trimmed, . . . and every officer his ''wedding-garment'' on? ''Shak.'', T. of the S., iv. 1. 51.}}

'''wedding-knife''' (wed′ing-nīf), ''n.'' One of a pair of knives contained in a sheath which is arranged to be worn at the girdle. This was a common
readings.c3s3:
wedding-gift in the seventeenth century.

'''wedding-ring''' (wed′ing-ring), ''n.'' A ring which is given by one of a married pair to the other on the occasion of their marriage, especially one given by the groom to the bride. It is usually a plain gold ring.

'''wedding-song''' (wed′ing-sông), ''n.'' A song sung in honor of a bride and groom; an epithalamium.

'''wede<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v. i.'' [ME. ''weden'', < AS. ''wēdan'', be mad, < ''wōd'', mad: see ''wood''<sup>2</sup>.] To go mad; rage; rave.
{{smaller block|<poem>He tok his leue & went home a-ȝeine
Weping as he wold ''wide'' for wo & for sorwe.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1509.}}}}

'''wede<sup>1</sup>†''', ''n.'' [ME., < ''wede'', ''v.''] Madness.
{{smaller block|<poem>And had therof so moche drede,
That he wende have go to ''wede''.</poem>
{{right|''MS. Harl.'' 1701, f. 24. (''Halliwell.'')}}}}

'''wede<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''weed''<sup>2</sup>.

'''wed-fee''' (wed′fē), ''n.'' [Also ''wedde-fee''; < ''wed'' + ''fee''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' A wager. ''Robson.'' (''Halliwell.'')

{{smaller block|The ''web-saw'', the glue-pot, the plane, and the hammer are the principal tools used.
{{right|''The Century'', XXXVII. 418.}}}}

As with other ME. forms in ''-ster'' (strictly fem. in themselves), the word was also often regarded as masc. (cf. ''baxter'' and ''brewster''<sup>1</sup>, used as masc. in ME.). The name survives in the surname ''Webster''.]   A weaver.   ''Wyclif'', Job vii. 6.
{{smaller block|One witness says “a very good ''webster'' can scarcely earne fower pence a day w<sup>th</sup> weavinge.”
{{right|''Record Soc. Lancashire and Cheshire'', XI. 53.}}}}

'''websterite''' (web′stėr-īt), ''n.''   [So named in honor of Thomas ''Webster'' (1772–1844), a Scottish geologist.]   Aluminite; hydrous tribasic sulphate of aluminium, found in Sussex, England, and at Halle in Prussia, in reniform masses and botryoidal concretions of a white or yellowish-white color.

'''Webster’s condenser.''' An apparatus consisting of two lenses, used in microscopy for intensifying the light thrown on the object.

'''web-toed''' (web′tōd), ''a.'' Web-footed.

'''web-wheel''' (web′hwēl), ''n.'' A wheel in which the hub and rim are connected by a web or plate, which may be either intact or perforated. {{smaller|It is a common form for railway car-wheels, and is also used for the wheels of watches and clocks, which are cast or stamped with webs, and then crossed out—that is, the web is perforated and filed into the form of spokes.   ''E. H. Knight.''}}

'''web-winged''' (web′wingd), ''a.'' Winged by large webs stretched between elongated digits of the fore limbs, as bats; chiropterous. See cuts under ''bat''<sup>2</sup> and ''Furia.''

'''web-worm''' (web′wėrm), ''n.'' Any one of several lepidopterous larvæ which feed more or less gregariously, and spin large webs into which they retire at night, or within which they feed during the day until the contained foliage is entirely devoured, when the web is enlarged. {{smaller|The tent-caterpillars, ''Clisiocampa americana'' and ''C. sylvatica'', are web-worms. (See cut under ''tent-caterpillar.'') The fall web-worm is the larva of the bombycid ''Hyphantria cunea.'' The garden web-worm is the larva of ''Eurycreon rantalis'', a pyralid moth of the family ''Botidæ.'' This species is not gregarious, but the larvæ form individual webs near the roots of corn, cotton, cabbage, melon, potato, and other cultivated crops in the western United States.—'''Grape web-worm.''' Same as ''vine inch-worm'' (which see, under ''vine'').—'''Turf web-worm.''' Same as ''sod-worm.''}}

'''wecht''' (weċht), ''n.''   [Also spelled ''weight, weght;'' perhaps connected with ME. ''weggen'', < AS. ''wecgan'', move, a secondary verb, < ''wegan'', carry: see ''weigh''<sup>1</sup>, and cf. ''weight''<sup>1</sup>.]   An instrument in the form of a sieve, but without holes, used for lifting grain.   ''Burns.'' [Scotch.]

'''wed†''' (wed), ''n.''   [= Sc. ''wad;'' < ME. ''wed, wedde,'' < AS. ''wed, wedd,'' a pledge, = OFries. ''wed'' = MD. ''wedde'' = OHG. ''wetti'', ''weti'', MHG. ''wette'', ''wete'', ''wet'', G. ''wette'' = Icel. ''veth'', a pledge, = Sw. ''vad'', a bet, appeal, = Goth. ''wadi'', a pledge, = L. ''vas'' (''vad-''), a pledge; cf. Gr. ἄεθλον, contr. ἆθλον (orig. *ἄϜεθλον), a prize, the prize of a contest (> ult. E. ''athlete'', etc.); cf. Skt. ''vadhū'', a bride, woman. Hence ''wed'', ''v.'', ''wadset'', etc. From the same source, L. or Teut., are ult. E. ''vadimony'', ''gage'', ''engage'', ''wage'', ''wager'', etc.]   A pledge; pawn; security.
{{smaller block|He that lawith at a mynstrels worde gevith to hym a ''wedde''.
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 31.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Passage shalt thou pai here under the grene-wode tre,
Or els thou shalt leve a ''wedde'' with me.</poem>
{{right|''Playe of Robyn Hode'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 427).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>There ’s nane that gaes by Carterhaugh
But maun leave him a ''wad'',
Either gowd rings, or green mantles.</poem>
{{right|''The Young Tamlane'' (Child’s Ballads, I. 115).}}}}
'''To wed''', in pledge; in pawn.
{{smaller block|A Kyng of Fraunce boughte theise Relikes somtyme of the Jewes, to whom the Emperour had leyde hem ''to wedde'', for a gret summe of Sylvre.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 13.}}}}
{{smaller block|Let him be war, his nekke lith ''to wedde''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 360.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>My londes beth set ''to wedde'', Robyn,
Untyll a certayne daye.</poem>
{{right|''Lytell Geste of Robyn Hode'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 54).}}}}

'''wed''' (wed), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''wedded'', ''wed'', ppr. ''wedding''.   [< ME. ''wedden'', < AS. ''weddian'', pledge, engage, = OS. ''weddian'' = MD. D. ''wedden'', lay a wager, = MHG. G. ''wetten'', wager, = Icel. ''vethja'', wager, = Sw. ''vädja'', appeal, = Dan. ''vedde'', wager, = Goth. ''ga-wadjōn'', pledge, betroth; from the noun. Cf. ''wage'', ''gage''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   I. ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To pledge; hence, to wager.
{{smaller block|<poem>Yee be welcome, that dare I wele ''wedde''.
My lorde has sente for to seke hym.</poem>
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 261.}}}}
{{smaller block|The yonge man, hauinge his hart all redy ''wedded'' to his frende Titus, . . . refused . . . to be parswaded.
{{right|''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, ii. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|I’ll ''wad'' a weather he’ll gar the blude spin frae under your nails. {{right|''Scott'', Black Dwarf, xvii.}}}}
'''2.''' To marry; take for husband or for wife.
{{smaller block|Thei ''wedden'' there no Wyfes; for alle the Wommen there ben commoun, and thei forsake no man.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 179.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Since the day
I saw thee first, and ''wedded'' thee.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ix. 1030.}}}}
'''3.''' To join in marriage; give or unite in wedlock.
{{smaller block|<poem>In Syracusa was I born, and ''wed''
Unto a woman. ''Shak.'', C. of E., i. 1. 37.</poem>}}
'''4.''' To unite closely in affection; attach firmly by passion or prejudice: as, to be ''wedded'' to one’s habits or opinions.
{{smaller block|Men are ''wedded'' to their lusts. ''Tillotson'', Sermons.
I am not ''wedded'' to these ideas.
{{right|''Jefferson'', To Colonel Monroe (Correspondence, I. 236).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Faith, fanatic Faith, once ''wedded'' fast
To some dear falsehood, hugs it to the last.</poem>
{{right|''Moore'', Lalla Rookh, Veiled Prophet.}}}}
'''5.''' To unite forever or inseparably.
{{smaller block|Thou art ''wedded'' to calamity. ''Shak.'', R. and J., iii. 3. 3.
<poem>They led the vine</poem>}}
{{smaller block|To ''wed'' her elm. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., v. 215.}}}}
'''6†.''' To espouse; take part with.
{{smaller block|They . . . ''wedded'' his cause. {{right|''Clarendon.''}}}}

''weddinghe''), wedding, marriage, verbal n. of ''weddian'', pledge, wed: see ''wed''<sup>1</sup>.]   Marriage; nuptials; nuptial ceremony or festivities, especially the latter: also used attributively: as, ''wedding'' cheer.
{{smaller block|There dide oure Lord the firste Myracle at the ''Wedyng'', whan he turned Watre in to Wyn.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 111.}}}}
{{smaller block|The kyngdam of heuenes is maad lic to a man kyng that made ''weddingus'' to his sone. {{right|''Wyclif'', Mat. xxii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Simple and brief was the ''wedding'', as that of Ruth and of Boaz.
Softly the youth and the maiden repeated the words of betrothal,
Taking each other for husband and wife in the Magistrate’s presence.</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', Miles Standish, ix.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Penny wedding''', a wedding at which the guests contribute toward the expenses of the entertainment, and frequently toward the household outfit of the wedded pair.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Love that no golden ties can attach
. . . will fly away from an Emperor’s match
To dance at a ''Penny Wedding!''</poem>
{{right|''Hood'', Miss Kilmansegg, Her Honeymoon.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Silver wedding, golden wedding, diamond wedding''', the celebrations of the twenty-fifth, the fiftieth, and the seventy-fifth anniversaries of a wedding, at which silver, gold, and diamond presents respectively are made. ''Paper, wooden, tin, crystal'', and ''china'' weddings are also sometimes celebrated on first, fifth, tenth, fifteenth, and twentieth anniversaries.}} ='''Syn.''' ''Nuptials, Matrimony'', etc. See ''marriage''.

'''wedge'''<sup>1</sup> (wej), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wegge, wigge, wege,'' < AS. ''wecg,'' a wedge (a mass of metal), = MD. ''wegghe, wigghe,'' D. ''wigge, wig,'' a wedge, = MLG. ''wegge'' = OHG. ''wekki, weggi,'' MHG. ''wecke, wegge,'' G. ''wecke, weck,'' a wedge-shaped loaf, = Icel. ''veggr'' = Sw. ''vigg'' = Dan. ''vægge,'' a wedge; prob. lit. ‘a mover’ (from the use and effect in splitting), ult. from the verb represented by ''weigh''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. Lith. ''wagis,'' a bent wooden peg for hanging {{img float|file=century v08 p0670 c3f1.png|width=60px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Wedge.}}}} things on, a spigot for a cask, also a wedge.]   '''1.''' A simple machine consisting of a very acute-angled triangular prism of hard material, which is driven in between objects to be separated, or into anything which is to be split. {{smaller|The wedge is merely a special application of an inclined plane, and is nowise entitled to a distinct place in the list of mechanical powers.}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
